steps.label: Place the product between −x² and x²
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the double inequality. It is the statement the Sandwich theorem is applied to, and it carries this mark.
lines: Multiply throughout by x², which is positive for x ≠ 0, so the inequalities keep their direction:

recall.must_convey: That sin(1/x) lies between −1 and 1, so multiplying by x² gives −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x².
accept: sine of one by x lies between minus one and one
multiply the inequality by x squared to get minus x squared and x squared
the product stays between minus x squared and x squared
sin one by x minus one and one madhya untundi

steps.why: sin(1/x) has no limit at x = 0, because 1/x increases without bound and the sine keeps oscillating between −1 and 1. That does not matter: the product still lies between two quantities that both approach 0.
common_mistakes: Writing lim(x → 0) sin(1/x) = 0; that limit does not exist.
Reversing the inequality signs when multiplying; x² is not negative, so they stay as they are.
steps.memory_tip: The sine factor stays between −1 and 1, so the product stays between −x² and x².

steps.label: Apply the Sandwich theorem
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the Sandwich theorem in words, then box 0. Both outer limits must be shown equal before the theorem can be used.
lines: The two outer limits are equal, so by the Sandwich theorem (also called the squeeze theorem) the expression between them has the same limit.

recall.must_convey: That both outer limits are 0, so by the Sandwich theorem the limit is 0.
accept: both outer limits are zero so by the sandwich theorem the answer is zero
apply the squeeze theorem and get zero
the sandwich theorem gives the limit zero

steps.why: The Sandwich theorem says that a function lying between two functions with the same limit L at a point has limit L there as well. Here both outer functions have limit 0.
common_mistakes: Writing 0 without naming the theorem; the name is what the method is credited for.
Splitting it as lim x² × lim sin(1/x); the product rule needs both limits to exist, and the second does not.
steps.memory_tip: When both outer limits are 0, the limit of the expression between them is 0 as well.
